Le bruit court dans certains cercles com:
Word is going around in some community circles. The City will have to compensate people who were subjected to racial profiling by the SPVM during police stops. While some welcome the news, others consider it insufficient. It excludes, for example, victims of racial profiling during traffic stops, cases that are far from isolated in Quebec. Our report.

On September 3, the Quebec Superior Court ordered the City of Montréal to compensate people who were victims of racial profiling during police stops carried out between August 2017 and January 2019, concluding that the City is responsible, as an employer, for the discrimination committed by its police officers. The decision follows a complaint filed against the City of Montréal by the Ligue des Noirs du Québec and Alexandre Lamontagne, a victim of racial profiling in August 2017.

The municipal administration has 30 days to appeal. If it doesn’t, victims of these stops made without valid grounds will be able to receive compensation ranging from $2,500 to $5,000.

The decision is a step forward, according to Max Stanley Bazin, president of the Ligue des Noirs. However, it doesn’t cover cases of racial profiling that occurred during traffic stops. Few studies precisely document this discrimination, but <l1>police ethics complaints</l1> dealing with situations of racism or racial profiling linked to traffic stops in Quebec rose from 68 in 2021-2022 to 103 in 2023-2024, an increase of 51.5%. That figure masks the scale of a phenomenon suffered by Montrealers who choose not to turn to the courts.
Ce n’est pas le cas de Pierre Fritzner,: That is not the case for Pierre Fritzner, who is currently waiting for the courts to rule on his complaint. His case concerns, precisely, a traffic stop and not a regular police stop, but he considers himself a victim of racial profiling. The same goes for several people who were stopped without cause while driving their vehicles but who will not be eligible for compensation, despite the injustice they feel they suffered. Traffic stops are different from regular police stops. Police officers who pull over drivers can do so without cause, as set out in section 636 of the Highway Safety Code. In 2022, however, a decision by Justice Yergeau of the Quebec Superior Court invalidated this provision in the Luamba case, finding that random traffic stops fostered situations of racial profiling. The case was appealed, and a decision has not yet been handed down as of this writing.
<strong>L’habitude d’être interpellé, un: Being used to getting stopped: a societal problem‍
Printemps 2021. Il est près de minuit, e: Spring 2021. It’s close to midnight, and Pierre Fritzner has just finished work, which keeps him at the office until late hours. He gets into his car and takes his usual route home, about twenty minutes away, toward the Villeray–Parc-Extension neighbourhood.
Selon ses dires, une voiture de police l: According to him, a police car spotted him, made a U-turn and followed him for several kilometres. “It happened three years ago, but I remember it like it was yesterday,” says the man in his sixties, who is of Haitian origin.
« J’étais fatigué, je conduisais douceme: “I was tired, I was driving slowly and carefully, but I knew I was being followed and that the officers were just waiting for me to commit an infraction so they could turn on their lights,” the Montrealer recounts. Then, as he expected, the red and blue lights of the police vehicle came on and moved closer, he says. He explains that he pulled over to the side of the street, making sure to stop at the corner of a large boulevard: “I was a Black man alone being pulled over at midnight. I wanted to be somewhere where people could see me, I didn’t want to be with police officers in a dark place that was hard to get to,” he says.
Selon lui, la police l’a questionné pend: According to him, the police questioned him for two hours: “Where are you coming from? Where are you going? Do you live around here? Why are you out driving at midnight?” Pierre Fritzner recalls. “I hadn’t done anything illegal, and they kept me waiting until 2 a.m. because I aroused a suspicion that, in all likelihood, is linked to my skin colour,” he says indignantly. The police allegedly let him go in the end with three tickets for minor infractions, including a rear light that no longer worked.
M. Fritzner est né et a grandi à Montréa: Mr. Fritzner was born and raised in Montréal. In the early 1980s, when he was only 16, the police, he says, kept stopping him. “I was so fed up that I even went to file a complaint at the police station. Then I realized it was absurd to try to file a complaint against the police with the police.”
Pour Pierre, tout cela est aberrant. « D: For Pierre, all of this is outrageous. “Stories like mine, there are thousands of them every year. I created a group, the Fondation des victimes de profilage racial, which brings together people who have experienced episodes similar to mine,” he says in closing. He believes that the Superior Court’s decision on September 3 favours change, but that it will take a long time before the police force stops discriminating against citizens.
<strong>Le prix à payer pour être indemn: The price to pay to be compensated
Dans les bureaux du Centre de recherche-: In the downtown offices of the Centre de recherche-action sur les relations raciales (CRARR), we meet Fo Niemi, co-founder and executive director of this nonprofit dedicated to defending civil rights. The CRARR works with lawyers who defend victims of racial injustice.
Face aux baies vitrées donnant sur la ru: Facing the floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking Sainte-Catherine Street, a few lawyers quietly work on their files, surrounded by stacks of paper.
« 5 000 $ d’indemnisation pour une victi: “$5,000 in compensation for a victim of racial profiling?” he begins. “If you were stopped, handcuffed, maybe even shoved around, and detained… $5,000?” he repeats, visibly indignant. “Human value is underestimated. The minimum compensation should be $10,000!” he exclaims.
Au-delà de la somme, c’est la lenteur du: Beyond the amount, it’s the slowness of the process that discourages many victims, Mr. Niemi points out: “The Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse can take up to three years to investigate and issue a decision. Then you sometimes have to wait another two years for the case to go before the Tribunal des droits de la personne and for a decision to be handed down.” Victims may therefore have to wait up to five years for compensation they consider insufficient. “Very few are willing to get into that much paperwork for so little,” he notes.
Pour beaucoup, l’attente devient aussi u: For many, the wait also becomes a psychological burden. “It’s very hard, because some people can’t move on. They’re constantly brought back to their case.” This is particularly true for young people, who often give up quickly. “The people who see it through to the end are generally between 30 and 45 years old. The younger ones lose motivation quickly.”
Une hausse du nombre de plaintes a tout: An increase in the number of complaints has nonetheless been observed since the beginning of 2024. “A complaint almost every two weeks,” says Fo Niemi, which is twice as many as before 2024. He can’t say precisely what explains the increase, but he is glad to see it and once again encourages everyone who is a victim of racial profiling to file a complaint.
<strong>Pour aller plus loin : que faire: Going further: what to do if you’ve been a victim of racial profiling?
M. Niemi a accepté de partager avec La C: Mr. Niemi agreed to share with La Converse his advice on the best way to proceed in the event of a police stop.
<strong>Rester calme durant une interpel: Stay calm during a police stop: “Even if you feel you’re being set up or provoked by police, it’s important to keep your cool. Don’t react with anger, because it could make the situation worse. Criminal charges of obstructing police could be laid against you,” Mr. Niemi warns.
<strong>Constituer des preuves :</strong: Gather evidence: “Film the scene immediately,” Mr. Niemi recommends. Record the situation without delay. Turn on your phone, because otherwise it will be your word against theirs.” If you can’t record what’s happening, discreetly call someone, such as a family member, and let them listen to the conversation live. This can prove very useful. “You’ll gain a witness to the scene,” he explains.
<strong>Consulter un médecin :</strong>: See a doctor: After the incident, it’s advisable to see a doctor, especially if you suffered physical or psychological injuries.
<strong>Ne pas se précipiter pour dépose: Don’t rush to file a complaint: “Wait at least a month before filing your complaint,” he advises. Writing a complaint too early can be a problem if criminal charges follow, because anything you write can then be used against you.
<strong>Déposer une plainte :</strong> V: File a complaint: You can file a complaint with the Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse or with the Commissaire à la déontologie policière.
<strong>Respecter les délais :</strong>: Respect the deadlines: If you did not suffer a physical injury, you have up to six months to file a complaint. If you were injured, the deadline can be up to three years. “Document every detail well,” Mr. Niemi reminds.
Massimiliano Mulone est criminologue de: Massimiliano Mulone is a criminologist by profession and an expert on the issue of racial profiling. In 2017, he was approached by the SPVM following numerous complaints filed by citizens about unequal treatment of members of racialized communities during stops carried out by the police force.
Mais qu’est-ce qu’une « interpellation »: But what does a “stop” mean in the context of racial profiling? “It’s similar to what you might call a ‘routine check.’ It’s not an arrest, but a situation that piques the officer’s interest. An offence isn’t necessary for an officer to stop a person, and the decision to stop someone depends entirely on the officer,” Mr. Mulone explains.
« Lors d’une interpellation, le policier: “During a stop, the officer has the right to identify and question the person they’re targeting without valid grounds,” he adds. And it is precisely this “without valid grounds” that is problematic, since it implies that an officer has the right to stop anyone, according to the expert.
Dans un <l1>rapport indépendant sur le S: In a 2019 <l1>independent report on the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal</l1> of which Mr. Mulone is one of the authors, one can read that “certain groups are more targeted by police stops. In fact, Indigenous people are six times more likely to be stopped by police than white people. Black people are stopped four times more than white people relative to their share of the population.” Arab or North African people, for their part, are 2.5 times more likely to be stopped.
À la suite de ces constats, le SPVM a di: Following these findings, the SPVM said it “humbly welcomes the results of the investigation and is committed to applying the experts’ recommendations and to bringing them back in order to understand the data that were collected.”
Mais, entre 2020 et 2023, rebelote : dan: But between 2020 and 2023, it was the same story again: in a <l1>second report</l1>, published in June 2023, the expert found the following: “The increase in stops affects all groups, but it is Indigenous people and Arab people who experienced, in relative terms, the largest increase.”
Fady Dagher, le chef de la police de Mon: Fady Dagher, Montréal’s police chief, acknowledged in court, in his testimony in this case, “the existence of racial profiling and systemic discrimination within the SPVM.” In February 2023, Mayor Valérie Plante, who also testified during the trial, said that the City recognized “the systemic nature of discrimination.”
Cependant, les experts estiment que, sur: However, experts believe that, on the ground, the problem lies in part in how police officers understand accusations of racism. “According to them, being racist requires an explicit intention to discriminate. They imagine, for example, that only a white supremacist, fully aware of and proud of his racist beliefs, could be labelled that way,” Mr. Mulone suggests.
Pourtant, des policiers peuvent discrimi: Yet police officers can discriminate without intending harm, he stresses: “It’s much more complex than that. Prejudice, implicit bias and structural discrimination can’t be reduced to deliberate acts.”
Le mardi 24 septembre, dans sa lettre de: On Tuesday, September 24, in his resignation letter obtained by Le Devoir, Commander Patrice Vilcéus also denounced systemic racism within the SPVM, calling the problem a “cancer eating away at the organization.”
<strong>Les interpellations policières,: Are police stops essential to our safety?
Selon le SPVM, les interpellations polic:
According to the SPVM, police stops are presented as necessary to public safety. The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal’s <l1>website</l1> states that their purpose is to “prevent incivilities” as well as “violations of laws and regulations.” However, “no scientific evidence supports this claim,” says Mr. Mulone.

These practices could even be counterproductive: “Disproportionately targeting individuals because of their skin colour creates a climate of insecurity among the population, particularly among minorities. This type of racial profiling generates tensions and harms the relationship of trust between law enforcement and the community (...) contributing to producing more insecurity, rather than preventing it.”
Dans ces conditions, comment limiter, vo: Under these conditions, how can we limit, or even stop, the stops that lead to episodes of profiling?
La principale recommandation du rapport: The report’s main recommendation is to impose a moratorium within the police service on stops without valid grounds. Accordingly, it says police should “voluntarily suspend any police stop that is not justified by the investigation of a specific crime or by reasonable suspicion of illegal activity.”
Pour Pierre Fritzner, Massimiliano Mulon: For Pierre Fritzner, Massimiliano Mulone and Fo Niemi, the finding is clear: the SPVM has many shortcomings.
« Même si les causes de ce problème sont: “Even if the causes of this problem run deeper,” Mr. Mulone continues, “an unfavourable ruling on police practices like stops without grounds, along with the bill for compensating victims of racial profiling, will surely push the City and its police service to rethink their practices.”
Questionné sur ce point, le SPVM s’est d: Asked about this, the SPVM said it was sensitive to the situation and confirmed that an analysis of the court decision was under way, in collaboration with the Service des affaires juridiques.
La Ville de Montréal n’a pas souhaité in: The City of Montréal declined to say whether it intended to appeal the September 3 decision, “[since it is] currently analyzing the judgment handed down.”
